issues.legal_issue: An outstill licence authorizing the manufacture and retail supply of country liquor grants an exclusive privilege rather than merely a licence for retail sale on the vendor’s premises.
material_facts: The licences authorized holders to manufacture country spirit in outstills and sell it by retail on their premises.
The holders could manufacture and sell without restrictions on the spirit’s strength or price, and each held a monopoly of manufacturing and supplying country liquor within the relevant area.
issues.conclusion: The licences granted an exclusive privilege within the meaning of section 22(1)(d), not merely licences within section 30.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 22(1)(d) of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act, 1915, the right to manufacture and supply country liquor as an exclusive privilege is distinct from a licence for retail sale on the vendor’s premises under section 30.

predicates.outstill_license_classification_case: The proceeding concerns the legal character of a licence to operate an outstill for country liquor.
predicates.licensee_may_manufacture_and_retail_sell: The licence holder is authorized to manufacture country spirit and sell it by retail on the holder’s premises.
predicates.licensee_has_area_supply_monopoly: The licence holder has a monopoly on manufacturing and supplying country liquor within the relevant area.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns an outstill licence that authorizes manufacture and retail sale and gives the holder an area supply monopoly, the licence grants an exclusive privilege.

issues.legal_issue: A licensee who cannot establish an outstill at a suitable site is not thereby entitled to remission, refund or compensation where the licensee remains responsible for finding a site and the licence remains in force.
material_facts: The auction notice placed responsibility for providing a location for the outstill on the successful bidder.
A licensee could not establish the outstill at the initially intended site and approval for another proposed site was withdrawn.
The licensee retained the licence and made further bids in subsequent years.

The licences were not cancelled or suspended under section 42, withdrawn under section 43, or surrendered in circumstances permitting remission under section 44(1); section 44(2) excluded that surrender provision for a licence to sell country liquor in exercise of an exclusive privilege.
issues.conclusion: The inability to locate and open the outstill did not excuse payment or entitle the licensee to remission, refund or compensation; the licences remained in force and section 45 barred a claim to compensation.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 42 and 43 provide for cancellation or suspension and withdrawal, with the statutory consequences described in the Act; section 44(1) permits surrender in specified cases, but section 44(2) excludes its application to a country-liquor sale licence exercising an exclusive privilege under section 22; section 45 precludes compensation while the licence remains in force. The auction conditions made site-finding the licensee’s responsibility.

rule.if: license_fee_remission_claim and licensee_is_responsible_for_finding_site and licensee_cannot_establish_shop and licence_remains_in_force

predicates.license_fee_remission_claim: The proceeding concerns a licensee’s claim to avoid or recover licence payments because the licensed shop was not established.
predicates.licensee_is_responsible_for_finding_site: The licensee, rather than the licensing authority, is responsible for finding a suitable site for the shop.
predicates.licensee_cannot_establish_shop: The licensee is unable to establish the shop at a suitable site.
predicates.licence_remains_in_force: The licence has not been cancelled, suspended, withdrawn or surrendered in a way that brings it to an end.

issues.definition: If a licensee responsible for finding a site cannot establish the shop but keeps the licence in force, that inability does not entitle the licensee to remission, refund or compensation.

issues.legal_issue: An instruction providing for return of an auction deposit when a licence is subsequently refused does not require return of the deposit when the licence was granted and was not subsequently refused.
material_facts: The relevant instruction concerned deposits made immediately as advance fees and provided for their return where a licence was subsequently refused for specified or other adequate reasons.
The licensee’s licence was granted and was not subsequently refused.
issues.conclusion: The instruction did not apply to the licensee’s claim for a refund; the Court did not decide the broader question whether the instruction was legally binding.
issues.legal_principle: The instruction addressed the return of deposits where a licence is subsequently refused, not the refund of payments under a licence that was granted and remained in force. The Court left open whether the instruction had binding legal force.

predicates.auction_deposit_refund_claim: The proceeding concerns a claim to return a deposit paid in connection with an auctioned licence.
predicates.licence_was_granted_and_not_subsequently: The licence was granted to the claimant and was not later refused.

issues.definition: Where a licence was granted and not later refused, a claim to return an auction deposit does not fall within an instruction limited to deposits for subsequently refused licences.

issues.legal_issue: The State may grant an exclusive privilege to manufacture and sell liquor for payment determined by public auction, and the payment is not refundable merely because there is no quid pro quo.
material_facts: The licences granted the exclusive privilege of manufacturing and selling country liquor.
The State fixed the amounts payable through public auction.
The licensees sought refunds on the ground that there was no quid pro quo for the sums collected.
issues.conclusion: The auction sums were payable as consideration for the exclusive privilege, and the absence of a quid pro quo did not entitle the licensees to a refund.
issues.legal_principle: Section 29 of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act, 1915 permits the State to accept payment in consideration of an exclusive privilege granted under section 22. Nashirwar v. State of Madhya Pradesh and Har Shankar v. Deputy Excise and Taxation Commissioner establish the State’s power to auction its exclusive liquor privilege and accept payment for it; auction is a means of ascertaining the best price.

predicates.exclusive_privilege_payment_case: The proceeding concerns payment demanded for a State-granted exclusive privilege to manufacture and sell liquor.
predicates.state_grants_exclusive_liquor_privilege: The State grants a person an exclusive privilege to manufacture and sell liquor.
predicates.payment_is_set_by_public_auction: The amount payable for the privilege is determined through a public auction.

issues.definition: When the State grants an exclusive liquor privilege for an amount set by public auction, that amount is payable consideration even without a separate quid pro quo.

issues.legal_issue: A licensee has no automatic right to a reduction of auction-set licence fees merely because the licence operated at a loss or the bids are alleged to have been speculative.
material_facts: The licensees sought reductions after alleging losses and claiming that rival bidders had made speculative bids.
They alleged that the auction officer should have refused the bids or stopped the bidding at a lower figure.
They relied on administrative instructions concerning speculative bidding and fee reductions.
The Board’s statutory authority to reduce fees was discretionary and applied during the unexpired portion of a grant.
issues.conclusion: The alleged losses and speculative bidding did not establish a right to fee reduction; the relevant instructions did not confer such a right, and the decision remained within the Board’s discretion.
issues.legal_principle: Section 39 of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act, 1915 gives the Board power, if it thinks fit, to reduce fees during the unexpired portion of a grant. The administrative guidance did not create a right to reduction or override that statutory discretion; a licensee is not entitled to reduction as of right merely because bidding proved unprofitable. The Court also observed that whether the stated circumstances existed was a factual question that could not be tried in those proceedings.

predicates.excise_licence_fee_reduction_claim: The proceeding concerns a licensee’s request to reduce fees payable for an excise licence.
predicates.licence_fee_was_set_by_auction: The licence fee was fixed through an auction.
predicates.licensee_claims_loss_or_speculative_bidd: The licensee alleges that operating the licence caused a loss or that bids at the auction were speculative.

issues.definition: A licensee who seeks reduction of an auction-set excise fee based on loss or alleged speculative bidding has no automatic right to that reduction.
